slides.title: Chapter 11: The Blockchain
slides.say: This deck explains what a block is, how blocks are chained and named, how a merkle tree summarises transactions, and how Bitcoin's test chains differ. Every number on a result picture was computed with the chapter's own Python library or read from one recorded run of Bitcoin Core 31.1.
slides.concept: How a block is built, how blocks are linked, how a merkle tree vouches for them, and which chain to test on

slides.title: Today's route
slides.say: The route has three parts that follow the order of the chapter. Four true stories and seventeen code examples are spread across them. The examples are listed in the same order in the chapter code tab of the course page, so every listing here can be run and edited there.
slides.concept: Three parts, seventeen examples, four true stories

slides.title: The questions this chapter answers
slides.say: The seven questions are the chapter's own, rewritten so that each has an answer on a slide. We return to them in the summary. A reader who can answer all seven has understood the chapter.
slides.concept: Each has an answer on a slide; we return to them in the summary

slides.title: One chapter, three parts
slides.say: The chapter has three parts and 41 key concepts. Each part gets a divider, concept cards with everyday comparisons, code that runs, and true stories. The deck follows the order of the chapter.
slides.concept: Three parts; every slide today lives on this map

slides.title: The block and the chain
slides.say: A block is a header of 80 bytes and a list of transactions. This part takes the header apart, shows how a block is named, and why changing one old block breaks every later one.
slides.concept: A chain is a train: every carriage is coupled to the one before it.

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (1 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover Structure of a Block, Block Header, Block Identifiers: Block Header Hash and Block Height and The Genesis Block. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A block is header, count, transactions
slides.say: The genesis block is the smallest block there is. Its header takes 80 bytes, a count byte says there is one transaction, and the transaction fills the rest. Bitcoin Core on a private chain reports the same total. It is example 1 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Header, count byte and transaction make the whole block

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (2 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover Linking Blocks in the Blockchain, blockchain, parent blocks and genesis block. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Six fields in 80 bytes
slides.say: Version, previous block, merkle root, time, bits and nonce always sit in the same places. Four plus thirty-two plus thirty-two plus three times four make eighty. That fixed size is what makes headers cheap to store and check. It is example 2 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Every header has the same six fields in the same order and widths

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (3 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover child blocks, blocks and block header hash. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Time, target and difficulty
slides.say: The time field counts seconds since 1970. Median time past takes the middle of eleven timestamps, so a single lying clock cannot move it. Bits packs the target, and difficulty compares it with the easiest target. It is example 3 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Bits is a compressed target; a smaller target means more difficulty

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (4 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover block height, Bitcoin Core and Nakamoto, Satoshi. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: The first block quotes a newspaper
slides.say: The creator wrote a newspaper headline into the first block. The block hash, found by trying nonces, starts with ten zero digits. That is the work that made the block expensive to forge. It is example 4 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: The ten zeros at the start of the name are the proof of work

slides.title: The Times in the first block
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2009-01-03. The genesis block of Bitcoin has the timestamp 1231006505, which is 18:15:05 UTC on 3 January 2009. The lesson is that a date quoted inside a block proves the block is not older.
slides.concept: A newspaper headline nailed into the first block

slides.title: The block and the chain: concepts (5 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover linking blocks in blockchain, BIP 34 and Bitcoin network. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Hash twice to get the name
slides.say: One SHA-256 gives a different value from the block's name. Only the second hash, taken over the first, equals the hash in the source code. Every node recomputes it, so no one has to trust a stored name. It is example 5 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: The name is computed again by every node; it is never stored in the block

slides.title: Height in the coinbase script
slides.say: Since BIP 34 the first bytes of the coinbase script spell the block height. We decode eight recorded scripts and get the heights back. Core refused to spend a reward after 99 confirmations and accepted it after 100. It is example 6 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: A newly mined reward cannot be spent until 100 blocks are on top of it

slides.title: Changing one block breaks the chain
slides.say: Each header holds the hash of its parent. Flip a single bit in header 3 and the link of header 4 no longer fits. To make the chain valid again, seven headers must be mined once more. It is example 7 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Alter block 3 and you must mine seven headers again

slides.title: A fork, and the odds of catching up
slides.say: Two blocks were mined on the same parent at height 511. One more block on the first child made it the active chain. The formula from the white paper shows how fast an attacker with ten percent falls behind. It is example 8 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: A fork ends when one branch grows longer; an attacker's odds fall fast

slides.title: Merkle trees
slides.say: A merkle tree squeezes thousands of transactions into one hash in the header. We build a small tree, follow a proof of a few hashes, and meet the weakness that comes from repeating the last hash.
slides.concept: A merkle tree is a knockout draw that ends with one winner, the root.

slides.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (1 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover Merkle Trees, Merkle Trees and Lightweight Clients, binary hash trees and balanced merkle trees. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Pair, hash, repeat
slides.say: Four transaction ids make two hashes, then one root. The root equals the value in the block header. With three ids the last one is repeated, which gives the same number of levels. It is example 9 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: An odd level is completed by pairing the last hash with itself

slides.title: Merkle trees: key concepts (2 of 2)
slides.say: These cards cover authentication path, merkle path and lightweight clients. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: A proof of four hashes
slides.say: To prove one transaction we hand over the sibling hash at each level. Following them upward rebuilds the root in the header. Doubling the block adds a single hash to the proof. It is example 10 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: The proof grows slowly: 16,000 transactions need 14 hashes

slides.title: Ralph Merkle's hash tree
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 1982-01-05. Ralph Merkle patented the hash tree in 1979, and the United States patent 4309569, Method of providing digital signatures, was published on 5 January 1982 with the Board of Trustees of Stanford University as assignee. The lesson is that a small summary can vouch for a large list.
slides.concept: One small hash that vouches for a whole list

slides.title: Two lists, one root
slides.say: Repeating the last two ids of six transactions gives the same root as the plain list. A block with such a copy therefore looks valid by its header. Core received one in a test and rejected it as a duplicate. It is example 11 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Core refuses a block whose transaction list repeats a hash

slides.title: A light client needs 248 bytes
slides.say: A light client asks a full node for a proof. It gets the header, the number of transactions, five hashes and some flags. Core confirmed that the proof contains exactly the transaction we asked about. It is example 12 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: A phone can check one payment without the other fifteen transactions

slides.title: Test blockchains
slides.say: Bitcoin has more than one chain. Testnet, signet and regtest follow the same rules with different constants, so developers can experiment without real money. We compare them and read their constants.
slides.concept: A test chain is a rehearsal room: same stage, no real audience.

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (1 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover Bitcoin's Test Blockchains, Testnet: Bitcoin's Testing Playground, Using testnet and Problems with testnet. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: One code base, five chains
slides.say: The constants of every chain live in one source file. Each chain listens on its own port. The size of the data a new node must fetch ranges from hundreds of gigabytes to nothing at all. It is example 13 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Each chain has its own port, so nodes of different chains never mix

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (2 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover Signet: The Proof of Authority Testnet, The default signet and custom signets, Regtest: The Local Blockchain and Using Test Blockchains for Development. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Testnet allows easy blocks
slides.say: Testnet, testnet4 and regtest allow a block at minimum difficulty. That keeps a small test chain moving, but it also let miners flood testnet3. Core's help text now calls testnet3 deprecated. It is example 14 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Two of the test chains may drop to the easiest difficulty after twenty minutes

slides.title: When the sandbox was flooded
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2024-05-04. On 4 May 2024 Jameson Lopp published Griefing Bitcoin's Testnet, which describes how the testnet3 rule of minimum difficulty after 20 minutes lets miners create hundreds of blocks in a single day. The lesson is that a test network without incentives needs rules against vandals.
slides.concept: A test network without incentives gets flooded

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (3 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover test blockchains, testnet and signet. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Addresses show the chain
slides.say: Mainnet addresses start with bc and legacy version byte 0. All test chains use tb, except regtest with bcrt, and version byte 111. A wallet can reject an address of the wrong chain at once. It is example 15 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: A testnet address can never be mistaken for a real one

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (4 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover default signet, custom signets and challenge script. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Signet: a challenge script
slides.say: The default signet asks for a signature from one of two keys. Its network magic comes from hashing that script, so a different challenge gives a different network. Challenge 51 means anyone can sign. It is example 16 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: The four magic bytes are the start of the hash of the challenge

slides.title: A test network with a doorman
slides.say: This is a true story, dated 2019-03-20. BIP 325, Signet, was assigned on 20 March 2019 to Karl-Johan Alm and Anthony Towns: a test network in which a block is valid only if it carries a solution to a challenge script, so that its creators decide who may make blocks.
slides.concept: Replace mining by a signature and the test network stays calm

slides.title: Test blockchains: key concepts (5 of 5)
slides.say: These cards cover regtest, BIP 325 and mainnet. Each pairs a short meaning with something from everyday life, so that the idea can be retold in your own words. The full explanation is on the course page, chapter 11.
slides.concept: Say each idea twice: once as the meaning, once as the everyday comparison

slides.title: Halving every 150 blocks
slides.say: On regtest the reward halves every 150 blocks, so the whole schedule can be tested in seconds. The library's rule, fed with this number, matches every height that Core recorded. It is example 17 in the chapter code tab of the course page.
slides.concept: Mine 500 blocks in seconds and see the reward halve three times
